n: The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see {{Psalm 116:5-7|Psalm 116:5–7}}). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.

This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is:

- righteous,

- gracious,

- compassionate,

- faithful,

- just,

- trustworthy,

- upright,

- holy, and

- awe-inspiring ({{Psalm 111:3|Psalm 111:3}}, {{Psalm 111:4|4}}, {{Psalm 111:7|7}}, {{Psalm 111:8|8}}, {{Psalm 111:9|9}}).

God's character gives hope in the covenant relationship ({{Psalm 111:5|Psalm 111:5}}). God rescued Israel from Egypt ({{Psalm 111:9|Psalm 111:9}}). God gave them the land ({{Psalm 111:6|111:6}}). God provides for his people ({{Psalm 111:5|111:5}}). However, God expects those in this relationship to also be righteous and have integrity.
The word *Hallelujah!* is repeated throughout this group of psalms.
God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing food. He remembers his covenant with Abraham (see {{Psalm 105:8-11|Psalm 105:8–11}}).

Giving Israel the land of other nations was just and good. The Lord was judging those nations and showing grace to Israel. However, if the Israelites do not live faithfully and with integrity, they will also lose the land. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.
The people of the exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.

True wisdom is the source of life ({{Proverbs 3:18|Proverbs 3:18}}; {{Proverbs 9:11|9:11}}; {{Ecclesiastes 7:12|Ecclesiastes 7:12}}). It starts with the fear of the Lord ({{Proverbs 9:10|Proverbs 9:10}}).

The fear of the Lord leads to a wise life that honors God and brings blessing to the family and the community. The godly follow God with joy. Their obedience does not come from fear like a slave obeying a master.

This psalm repeats the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord ({{Psalm 111:1-10|Psalm 111}}). Wise people have reasons to be happy ({{Psalm 112:1-5|Psalm 112:1–5}}) and strong ({{Psalm 112:6-10|112:6–10}}).

*blessed*: Everyone will recognize the children of godly people (see {{Psalm 127:4|Psalm 127:4}}) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see {{Psalm 1:3|1:3}}; compare {{Matthew 6:20|Matthew 6:20}}).

Godly people imitate God by being generous, compassionate, and righteous ({{Psalm 51:1|Psalms 51:1}}; {{Psalm 111:1-10|111:1–10}}; {{2 Corinthians 9:9|2 Corinthians 9:9}}). They lend money to the poor without charging interest ({{Psalm 15:5|Psalms 15:5}}; {{Psalm 112:9|112:9}}; {{Exodus 22:25|Exodus 22:25}}).

The wise avoid mistakes because they are honest and compassionate ({{Psalm 15:5|Psalms 15:5}}; {{Psalm 37:23-24|37:23–24}}). People will remember them for a long time ({{Proverbs 10:7|Proverbs 10:7}}).
Because the godly trust that God will rescue them and give them victory, they face their enemies with confidence ({{Psalm 59:10|Psalms 59:10}}; {{Psalm 112:4|112:4}}; {{Psalm 118:7|118:7}}).
Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving ({{2 Corinthians 9:9|2 Corinthians 9:9}}).

- The wicked *gnash their teeth* in anger due to their bitter envy ({{Psalm 35:16|Psalms 35:16}}; {{Psalm 37:12|37:12}}). The strength and reputation of the godly create conflict with those who wish them harm. 

- The wicked will retreat in fear and shame.

*the name of the LORD*: God's personal name (Hebrew *Yahweh;* see {{Exodus 3:15|Exodus 3:15}}) reveals who he is (his nature, character, and reputation). He is exalted at all times (now and forever) and in every place (from east to west).

This song of praise celebrates the greatness of the Lord's name and glory. God is exalted and glorious in heaven ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}). He also stoops down to care for the lowly and needy on earth ({{Psalm 113:5-9|Psalm 113:5–9}}).

These psalms are called the Egyptian Hallel. *Hallel* means “praise.” Jewish people use these psalms during Passover, which began when God brought Israel out of Egypt in the exodus. The people recite {{Psalm 113:1-114:8|Psalms 113–114}} before the Passover meal, and {{Psalm 115:1-118:29|Psalms 115–118}} are recited afterward.

The Lord’s glory extends to the heavens ({{Psalm 57:5|Psalms 57:5}}, {{Psalm 57:11|11}}; {{Psalm 99:2|99:2}}; {{Psalm 108:5|108:5}}; {{Psalm 138:6|138:6}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}) and throughout the world of human relationships.
The Lord is unlike anyone else, yet he personally cares for people on earth.
The Lord humbles himself to connect directly with his people (see {{Psalm 138:6|Psalm 138:6}}; {{Philippians 2:6-8|Philippians 2:6–8}}).
These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise ({{1 Samuel 2:8-9|1 Samuel 2:8–9a}}).

- People in this culture often treated a woman without children with shame or contempt ({{Genesis 16:4|Genesis 16:4}}). But the Lord has the power to make her a happy mother. For example: 

- Sarah ({{Genesis 21:2|Genesis 21:2}}),

- Rebekah ({{Genesis 25:21|Genesis 25:21}}),

- Rachel ({{Genesis 30:23|Genesis 30:23}}), and

- Hannah ({{1 Samuel 1:20|1 Samuel 1:20}}).

- God's greatness and goodness give people many reasons to praise him.

- At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the promised land, Israel was one holy kingdom ({{Exodus 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5–6}}). 

- The mention of Judah and Israel as separate lands shows the psalm was written after the kingdom was divided ({{1 Kings 12:16-17|1 Kings 12:16–17}}; compare {{1 Samuel 11:8|1 Samuel 11:8}}; {{1 Kings 1:35|1 Kings 1:35}}), and probably after the exile. Judah became God's sanctuary because the people worshiped God there. His tabernacle, and later his temple, were located there.

This song celebrates the Lord's power in nature. It remembers Israel's start as a nation during the exodus ({{Psalm 114:1-2|Psalm 114:1–2}}) and their entry into the promised land ({{Psalm 114:3-6|114:3–6}}). It encourages respect for the God of Jacob ({{Psalm 114:7-8|Psalm 114:7–8}}).

- *fled*: God parted the waters so that Israel could escape Egypt ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalm 77:17–18}}; {{Exodus 14:1-31|Exodus 14}}). 

- The Jordan River *turned back* when Israel arrived to cross it (see {{Joshua 3:1-17|Joshua 3}}). 

- *skipped like rams*: God's presence made the mountains quake ({{Exodus 19:16-20|Exodus 19:16–20}}).
The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the exodus.
The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

This is a song of thanksgiving for God's blessings. The community gives all glory to the Lord, the true source of hope and blessing. Those who trust in idols feel great disappointment. The Creator's blessing extends to future generations ({{Psalm 115:14|Psalm 115:14}}), especially to the priests ({{Psalm 115:12|115:12}}).

*Where is their God?*: People question God's presence or power when he does not act as they expect (compare {{Psalm 14:1|Psalms 14:1}}; {{Psalm 42:3|42:3}}, {{Psalm 42:10|10}}). However, God is in the heavens. He has all power, authority, and knowledge. He does as he wishes, not what people think he should do. He carries out his plans according to his will ({{Ephesians 1:11|Ephesians 1:11}}) and acts in his own time and ways.

- This entire section is repeated in {{Psalm 135:15-20|Psalm 135:15–20}}. 

- Unlike the Lord ({{Psalm 95:3-5|Psalm 95:3–5}}), idols cannot do anything. They are useless.
Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those who trust in them ({{Isaiah 44:20|Isaiah 44:20}}).

*Israel … O house of Aaron … You who fear the LORD*: The psalmist urges everyone in the God-fearing community to trust in the living God. This threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true helper and shield (compare {{Psalm 118:2-4|Psalm 118:2–4}}).
The groups mentioned in {{Psalm 115:9-11|Psalm 115:9–11}} receive assurance of the Lord's blessing, no matter their social status (see {{Psalm 113:8|113:8}}).

- The psalmist blesses ({{Psalm 107:37-38|Psalm 107:37–38}}, {{Psalm 107:41|41}}) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. 

- *the Maker of heaven and earth*: This phrase speaks about how the Lord created everything and has power over all creation.

- *The highest heavens belong to the LORD*: God's exaltation starts in heaven ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}), far above the gods of other nations. The earth also belongs to him ({{Psalm 47:9|Psalm 47:9}}; {{Psalm 95:4|95:4}}). 

- The dead cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living praise God in thanksgiving for his blessings ({{Psalm 79:13|Psalm 79:13}}).
*I love the LORD*: This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see {{Psalm 18:1|Psalm 18:1}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:5|Deuteronomy 6:5}}) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.

Psalm 116 is a poem that gives thanks to God. The speaker explains why they love God. It’s because God heard their cry for help and took action to save them.

This psalm has many things in common with Psalm 22. First, the speaker recognises things that are true about God. This includes God being full of tender love. Second, the speaker describes how they felt when they were suffering. They were sad, terrified and in great pain. Third, the speaker trusted in God even when they were facing danger.

What is different from Psalm 22 is that God has already rescued the speaker. That is why they are thanking God. They show that they are thankful in many ways. They worship God and offer a sacrifice. They tell others what God has done for them. They keep their promises to God and serve him faithfully.

This song of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death ({{Psalm 116:1-11|Psalm 116:1–11}}). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly ({{Psalm 116:12-19|Psalm 116:12–19}}).
Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people({{Psalm 107:41|Psalm 107:41}}; {{Psalm 113:6-8|113:6–8}}), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
It is not clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s name (which represents God's reputation).
The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see {{Psalm 111:1-5|Psalm 111:1–5}}) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
People with childlike faith readily receive God's wisdom and instruction ({{Psalm 19:7-11|Psalm 19:7–11}}; {{Matthew 18:3-4|Matthew 18:3–4}}).
The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had suffered, the Lord was faithful. However, people are all liars.

*I will walk before the LORD*: The psalmist lived with integrity. After experiencing deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see {{Psalm 56:13|Psalm 56:13}}; compare {{Job 42:5|Job 42:5}}).
*I believed*: Paul quotes this phrase in {{2 Corinthians 4:13|2 Corinthians 4:13}}.

- The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude.

- All he has done for the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life.

- The *cup of salvation* overflows with God’s blessings ({{Psalm 23:5|Psalm 23:5}}), unlike the cup of judgment ({{Psalm 75:8|75:8}}). 

- The psalmist makes *vows* ({{Psalm 116:18|Psalm 116:18}}) to praise the Lord publicly ({{Psalm 116:17-18|116:17–18}}).
No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.
Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel ({{Romans 15:11|Romans 15:11}}).
This psalm is the shortest in the Psalter. It invites all people of the earth to praise the Lord for his *loving devotion and faithfulness.*

The psalmist joyfully thanks the Lord for his goodness and urges others to trust in his *loving devotion* ({{Psalm 118:1-4|Psalm 118:1–4}}, {{Psalm 118:29|29}}). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel ({{Psalm 113:1-118:29|Psalms 113–118}}).
*Israel … the house of Aaron … those who fear the LORD*: These three groups represent the entire covenant community (compare {{Psalm 115:9-11|Psalms 115:9–11}}; {{Psalm 135:19-20|135:19–20}}).
The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.

- *The LORD is on my side*: Compare {{Romans 8:31|Romans 8:31;}} {{Hebrews 13:6|Hebrews 13:6}}. 

- God's presence removes the need to fear people ({{Psalm 56:11|Psalm 56:11}}). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue ({{Psalm 59:10|Psalm 59:10}}; {{Psalm 112:8|Psalm 112:8}}).
Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders ({{Psalm 118:6|Psalms 118:6}}; {{Psalm 146:3|146:3}}).

- Strength comes from *the name of the LORD*. This is shown by the threefold repetition of the attackers, the *name of the LORD*, and the victory he gives.

- Even when hostile people surrounded the psalmist, the Lord *extinguished them like burning thorns* (see {{Isaiah 9:18|Isaiah 9:18}}; {{Isaiah 10:17|10:17}}).
The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s strong *right hand,* which kept him from death.
God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (see {{Psalm 116:6|Psalm 116:6}}, {{Psalm 116:12-19|12–19}}).

The *cornerstone* shapes and supports a building or arch. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord selects and places this stone for his sanctuary ({{Isaiah 28:16|Isaiah 28:16}}). 

Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone ({{Matthew 21:42|Matthew 21:42}}; {{Mark 12:10-11|Mark 12:10–11}}; {{Luke 20:17|Luke 20:17}}; see {{Acts 4:11|Acts 4:11}}; {{Ephesians 2:20|Ephesians 2:20}}; {{1 Peter 2:6-7|1 Peter 2:6–7}}).
The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.
*This is the day that the LORD has made*: The Lord's victory has begun, but it will be completed on another day ({{Psalm 118:25|Psalm 118:25}}).
The psalmist ends with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

- The one who comes in the name of the Lord brings the Lord’s complete victory (see {{Psalm 118:10-12|Psalm 118:10–12}}). 

- When Jesus triumphantly entered Jerusalem, the crowds shouted blessings. They used phrases from this verse ({{Matthew 21:9|Matthew 21:9}}; {{Mark 11:9|Mark 11:9}}; {{Luke 19:38|Luke 19:38}}; {{John 12:13|John 12:13}}). 

Jesus quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem ({{Matthew 23:39|Matthew 23:39}}; {{Luke 13:35|Luke 13:35}}).

Wise people are happy. They have integrity (see {{Psalm 84:11|Psalm 84:11}}) and follow God's guidance. They obey God's teachings and seek them with complete devotion (see {{Psalm 27:7|Psalm 27:7}}; {{Psalm 119:10|119:10}}, {{Psalm 119:45|45}}, {{Psalm 119:94|94}}, {{Psalm 119:155|155}}). They reject all evil forms. Compare {{Psalm 1:1-2|Psalm 1:1–2}}.

*Aleph* (א) is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 is written as an acrostic poem. Each section has eight verses, and every verse in that section begins with the same Hebrew letter. The first section begins with *Aleph*.

God, the author of these instructions, commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

Psalm 119 talks about the Mount Sinai covenant as a blessing for God’s people. It praises God for how wonderful his laws are. These are the laws recorded in the Law of Moses. Obeying them leads to wisdom, joy and life.

The poem is divided into 22 sections. Each section has eight verses. At the beginning of each section there is a word in the Hebrew language. These are the names of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 is an alphabet poem.

This psalm blends wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. It often uses eight Hebrew words translated as: 

- “Instructions” 

- “law” 

- “words” 

- “commandments”

- “statutes”

- “judgments”

- “promises” 

- “precepts“

These words encourage love for and obedience to God's instructions in the Scriptures (see {{2 Timothy 3:14-17|2 Timothy 3:14–17}}). A deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
To keep God’s commandments means to guard them by obeying them.

- A young person often acts foolishly ({{Proverbs 22:15|Proverbs 22:15}}) and can easily make mistakes that ruin their life ({{Proverbs 7:6-23|Proverbs 7:6–23}}). However, youth is the best time to build self-discipline and seek wisdom (see {{Psalm 34:11|Psalm 34:11}}; {{Proverbs 1:4|Proverbs 1:4}}). 

- *keep his way pure*: This means avoiding corruption by evil and sin and developing the integrity described in {{Psalm 15:1-5|Psalm 15}}.

*Beth* (ב) is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It makes the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist is determined to stay pure and encourages gaining wisdom through God's principles ({{Psalm 119:9|Psalm 119:9}}) and instructions ({{Psalm 119:10-16|119:10–16}}).
The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not stray.
God's wisdom is more valuable than any wealth people desire ({{Psalm 119:72|Psalm 119:72}}, {{Psalm 119:127|127}}; {{Proverbs 3:14-15|Proverbs 3:14–15}}).
The path of wisdom involves thinking deeply about God's teachings (see {{Psalm 119:1|Psalm 119:1}}, {{Psalm 119:3|3}}). Wise people consider the meaning of God's word.

The psalmist wants to live a life full of praise and obedience to please the Lord ({{Psalm 118:17|Psalms 118:17}}; {{Psalm 119:25|119:25}}, {{Psalm 119:77|77}}, {{Psalm 119:116|116}}, {{Psalm 119:144|144}}, {{Psalm 119:175|175}}). Only the Lord can remove his enemies and help him understand the wonderful truths in God's teachings.

*Gimel *(ג) is the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

Like a stranger in a hostile land, God's servant needs God's guidance.
The arrogant are probably those who mock the psalmist (Psalm {{Psalm 119:22-23|119:22–23}}).
Those who meditate on God’s instructions receive wise advice from them.

*Daleth *(ד) is the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The poet feels deep pain and sadness but asks the Lord to give him strength. He wants to follow the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s discipline ({{Psalm 118:17-18|Psalms 118:17–18}}; {{Psalm 119:67|119:67}}, {{Psalm 119:71|71}}, {{Psalm 119:75|75}}), but his instruction renews the weary soul (see {{Psalm 119:12|119:12}}).

- *path of deceit*: Self-deception comes from sinful human nature ({{Jeremiah 17:9|Jeremiah 17:9}}). It leads to foolishness. 

- Access to God’s word is a privilege, not a right.

*He *(ה) is the fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
The love for money can lead to sin (compare {{Exodus 18:21|Exodus 18:21}}; {{1 Timothy 3:1-5|1 Timothy 3:1–5}}; {{1 Timothy 6:10|6:10}}).
The psalmist asks for protection from enemies who speak harshly (see {{Psalm 42:10|Psalms 42:10}}; {{Psalm 44:16|44:16}}; {{Psalm 89:50-51|89:50–51}}; {{Psalm 102:8|102:8}}).

*Waw* (ו) is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his love and salvation.
The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
The psalmist finds joy in God's word despite experiencing pain ({{Psalm 119:92|Psalm 119:92}}, {{Psalm 119:143|143}}).

*Zayin *(ז) is the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist asks God to remember his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
*judgments of old*: This refers to God’s just rulings or decisions (his laws). These are found in the Torah, the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

*Heth *(ח) is the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist seeks God’s favor and loving devotion. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
Wicked people try to lead him into sin, but the psalmist remembers God's word and stays strong (see {{Psalm 119:16|Psalm 119:16}}).
God's goodness fills the earth. The entire creation shows evidence of his goodness (see {{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}}; {{Isaiah 11:9|11:9}}).

- *Good judgment and knowledge *come from wisdom ({{Psalm 111:10|Psalm 111:10}}). 

- The psalmist admits he used to wander like a lost sheep ({{Psalm 119:176|Psalm 119:176}}). 

- *now I keep your word*: See {{Psalm 119:25-29|Psalm 119:25–29}}. 

- *You are good, and You do what is good*: God's character is perfect ({{Psalm 97:2|Psalm 97:2}}; {{James 1:17|James 1:17}}; {{1 John 1:5|1 John 1:5}}).

*Teth *(ט) is the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist admits his sin and gratefully accepts the Lord's discipline.
As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.

*Yodh *(י) is the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.

*Kaph *(כ) is the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist feels exhausted from waiting for the Lord, but he still hopes for God's future rescue.
God's word is trustworthy. This contrasts with the lies of the enemies who hunt the psalmist without reason (see {{Psalm 119:78|Psalm 119:78}}).

*Lamedh *(ל) is the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
The wicked planned to kill the psalmist, but they faced destruction themselves ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).
*I have seen a limit to all perfection*: Humans cannot fully understand God's ways (see {{Ecclesiastes 3:11|Ecclesiastes 3:11}}).
*make me wiser*: God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.

*Mem *(מ) is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far better than the best that human teachers can offer.

- Wisdom is better than the finest food ({{Psalm 19:10|Psalm 19:10}}; {{Psalm 81:16|81:16}}). 

- The psalmist had already turned away from the false promises of foolishness (see {{Psalm 119:18|Psalm 119:18}}, {{Psalm 119:78|78}}, {{Psalm 119:86|86}}, {{Psalm 119:163|163}}).

The Lord’s word is like a lamp. It offers perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness ({{Psalm 18:25-29|Psalm 18:25–29}}; {{Psalm 119:130|119:130}}). This light also gives life ({{Proverbs 6:23|Proverbs 6:23}}).

*Nun *(נ) is the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist's deep commitment to God's word comes from within ({{Psalm 119:112|Psalm 119:112}}) and directs his actions.

- *freewill offerings of my mouth*: This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (compare {{Psalm 50:23|Psalm 50:23}}).

- The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
The godly hate the wicked and their actions ({{Psalm 5:4-6|Psalm 5:4–6}}; compare {{Ezekiel 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11}}).

*Samekh *(ס) is the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.

*Ayin *(ע) is the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The servant of the Lord struggles to endure the evil around him. He confidently asks the Lord to rescue him right away!
Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives discernment will he understand it.

*Pe *(פ) is the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.

*Tsadhe *(צ) is the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
The psalmist feels angry (compare {{Psalm 69:9|Psalm 69:9}}) because he sees wicked people ignoring God's word.
The psalmist feels very troubled by those who oppress him (see {{Psalm 119:143|Psalm 119:143}}; compare {{Isaiah 53:1-12|Isaiah 53}}).
*I rise* and *anticipate* translate the same Hebrew verb.

*Qoph* (ק) is the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Even when God seems distant, he is actually close.
*Coming to attack me* (or *draw near*) is a Hebrew wordplay on *You are near*. The wicked stay far from God's instructions, but the psalmist stays close, so he does not need to fear.
Resh (ר): This request for life appears throughout {{Psalm 119:1-176|Psalm 119}}, but it is focused in this stanza.

- *my heart fears … I rejoice*: Fear, trembling, and joy show the psalmist’s devotion to God. 

- God’s word is a treasure (*great spoil*). 

- In the Old Testament, the number seven represents wholeness.

*Shin *(ש) is the twenty-first letter of the alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.

*Taw *(ת) is the twenty-second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God's servant asks the Lord for help one last time. He still feels like a lost sheep.
God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his lost sheep ({{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}; {{Luke 15:4-6|Luke 15:4–6}}).
The psalmist is surrounded by liars, so he makes his lament to the Lord, the only one who can help him.

This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.

These short and memorable songs were sung by pilgrims as they traveled to Jerusalem for the national festivals held three times each year ({{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}}). The title of these psalms includes a Hebrew word that can mean “steps” or “stairs.” Some scholars understand it to mean “going up to Jerusalem.” These psalms, often called the Songs of Ascents, lead the listener on a journey to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel through history.

- The psalmist speaks with the liars around him. He feels confident that the Lord will judge them. 

- The Divine Warrior (see {{Psalm 7:12-13|Psalms 7:12–13}}; {{Psalm 11:4-6|11:4–6}}) will attack the liars with sharp arrows and burning coals.

Meshech was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. Kedar was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both places. 

Meshech was known for its slave trade ({{Ezekiel 27:13|Ezekiel 27:13}}; see also {{Exodus 21:16|Exodus 21:16}}), and Kedar was known for its warriors ({{Isaiah 21:16-17|Isaiah 21:16–17}}). These places represented the rebellious and violent land where the psalmist suffered.
The psalmist feels the pain of being alone, isolated, and in constant conflict.
